chapter_theme: Two songs at Thanichayam (தனிச்சயம்) in Kongu: the poet's own lovemaking and a wish that this birth end, with Murugan as the one who commanded him to sing the Thiruppugazh; and old age with its contempt and the hour of dying.

954.reading: The poet describes lovemaking frankly, giving betel, embracing, making bird-cries, kissing the neck, biting the lips and toiling without shame until his life is exhausted, and asks whether this birth of union, in which virtue is lost, will not end. The praise names Murugan who commanded him to sing the good Thiruppugazh with its lordship, poetic gift and authority of a guru, the one with the cock-banner, the most able of the able who teaches Siva and Agastya the grammar and literature of the three Tamils, at Thanichayam in the west.
954.nuance: The book names itself: குறித்த நற் றிருப்புகழ் ... எனைப் பணித்து அருள்வோனே, Murugan as the one who set the poet to sing. அறத் தவித்து: the union is the loss of dharma, and the plea is that the birth itself, not only the habit, end.

955.reading: The poet pictures the body's ruin in old age: its once-proud form shrivels, black hair whitens like cotton, the ears go deaf, the eyes blind, the teeth loosen, cough and phlegm rise, the head reels with bile, the body rots worse than a bloodless worm, mind, deeds and speech run out of bounds, the wife who came reviles him, all call him unclean, sense fails and the pulse is barely there; on that day of the soul's distress he asks for grace. The praise is a battle in drum syllables where ghouls drink blood from skulls and kites pull entrails, and names Murugan the lord of Vayalur and of Thanichayam in Kongu.
955.nuance: The decay is listed from the outside in, ending in துடிப்பதும் சிறிது உளது இலது, a pulse barely there or gone. அவத்தை here is the soul's distress at death. தடச்சிகண்டியில் in the last lines is unclear.

links.note: Both name Murugan's command to sing the Thiruppugazh: 2 remembers the grace of being told to sing, and 954 adds that the command came with lordship, poetic gift and a guru's authority.

Both picture the old man whose teeth are gone and whose body is scorned; the Naladiyar faults him for keeping his eyes on desire still, while 955 lists the decay and asks only for grace at the hour of death.
